items.title: Claude Code regularly sends each background agent’s transcript to its model
items.summary: Article URL: https://gist.github.com/flamerix-ai/c3905705cc4205e5de3011fa2e74efce Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50284255 Points: 355 # Comments: 115
items.content:
Tested on Linux, Claude Code 2.1.257–2.1.312 (see Tested versions). The binary is not modified ( BUN_OPTIONS=--preload ). An update can silently undo it, so see Verify.

To make it permanent for every Claude Code process, see Install .

Every ~30 seconds, for every background agent, Claude Code sends that agent's entire transcript to the agent's own model (usually Opus) and asks it to "describe your most recent action in 3-5 words". The answer only updates the agent's status line in the agents panel; it never reaches the model or your conversation. There is no setting that turns it off, and since 2.1.232 (August 2026) it has been on by default.

The anomaly was detected by DRIM in Claude Code's OpenTelemetry export: grouping claude_code.api_request events by query_source showed agent_summary costing more than the main conversation itself .

Spend here means Claude Code's own per-request estimate ( cost_usd ), not an invoice: on a subscription, what you lose is rate-limit headroom. We are not the only ones who measured it: #86879 collects four independent measurements of 18–26 %.

no-agent-summary.js is a Bun preload (~80 lines of code). It wraps setTimeout / setInterval ; when a callback's source text contains a summarizer anchor (e.g. the [AgentSummary] Timer fired log line), it returns an inert handle instead of arming the timer. Every other timer passes through untouched. In the OpenTelemetry export the suppressed requests are claude_code.api_request events with query_source = agent_summary .

Why a timer hook rather than something simpler: the module ships as precompiled Bun bytecode, so editing its JS text inside the binary changes nothing, and the API client does not go through a wrapped globalThis.fetch . But Function.prototype.toString still returns a callback's source even when it runs from bytecode, so the timer can be recognised by a string inside it. The inert timer uses exactly 2³¹−1 ms: Node and Bun treat a larger delay as 1 ms, so an "infinite" delay would fire at once.

Put no-agent-summary.js somewhere stable; note its absolute path.

Set BUN_OPTIONS globally so every Claude Code process gets it. One of:

Or a wrapper named claude earlier on PATH (the case keeps it idempotent when one Claude Code process starts another):

Restart the daemon and every already-running session, then start Claude Code from an environment that has BUN_OPTIONS :

Expect preload active mode=off … . No line: BUN_OPTIONS did not reach the process, or the path is not absolute.

Timer suppressed: with the same BUN_OPTIONS and CC_AGENT_SUMMARY_LOG=/tmp/nas.log , run a background subagent for a minute or two. The log shows summary timer #1 suppressed (setTimeout, delay=30000) and the agent's panel status stops updating. If you export OpenTelemetry, query_source = agent_summary should stay at zero; this is the only check that catches every failure mode.

Matching is by source text : an anchor must sit inside the callback passed to the timer. If an update breaks that, the hook matches nothing and summaries silently come back. Ways it can happen:

Linux x64 binary from npm @anthropic-ai/claude-code-linux-x64 (its sha256 equals the native installer's manifest.json checksum). Static: the extracted bundle's summary timer callback carries a hook anchor. Live: claude -p --model haiku with CLAUDE_CODE_AGENT_PROGRESS_SUMMARIES=1 , one subagent doing 8 steps of ~20 s, counting [AgentSummary] Forking in --debug-file .

5 / 5 / 0 = the fork happens on this version, merely loading the hook changes nothing, and off removes it.

In our telemetry its weekly share of spend went from 3.5–7 % in July (the fork gate was already open for us) to 7.3 % and then 11.8 % in the week we picked up 2.1.233, and to about 16 % by mid-October.

items.title: 'Like cutting up a Picasso': AI microdrama edit of Neighbours worries actors and crew
items.summary: A micro-drama will use AI-assisted technology to edit old episodes of the Australian TV soap to focus on Margot Robbie's character.
items.content:
Former Neighbours actors and crew have raised concerns about plans to use AI to help re-edit old footage and make mini episodes for mobile phone viewers.

Fremantle, producer of the now-defunct Australian TV soap opera, has partnered with US-based RoseBerry Media for the project that will use AI to "scan decades of episodes" to help make short vertical videos.

Footage of Margot Robbie, who played Donna Freedman from 2008 to 2011, will be the initial focus of the micro-drama.

Both companies say the move will bring the show - which aired its final episode last year - to new audiences. But some actors and crew say they have not consented to their images, voice or work to be re-purposed.

Robbie has yet to respond publicly. The BBC has contacted her agency for comment.

In a statement, the companies behind the project said the AI-assisted technology will "scan decades of episodes to map character arcs, storylines and standout moments, helping editors quickly identify the strongest material".

The micro-drama episodes will use "original, previously broadcast footage, dialogue and performances", according to Fremantle spokesman.

"It does not generate new scenes or performances, alter actors' faces or likenesses, or use synthetic voices," he said, adding that a human editor would be "reviewing and approving every stage of the editing process".

The mini episodes will likely feature Matt Werkmeister, 34, who joined the set of Neighbours in 2005 when he was 13 years old. He played a regular character, Zeke Kinski and shared many scenes with Robbie's character.

Now a Melbourne-based producer and director, Werkmeister says he hasn't been approached by the companies behind the micro-drama and is concerned what the episodes will feature.

"If they're creating a new micro-drama out of something that already exists, I feel there needs to be consent for using our image and voice as well as the writers," he said.

Robbie is "obviously a big draw card" and "it's nice to watch old clips from shows you used to watch," Werkmeister said, but when he signed his contract two decades ago, "streaming didn't even exist as a platform" so he's unsure of what his rights are.

That uncertainty is also at the forefront of Sam Clark's mind. He played Ringo Brown on Neighbours from 2006 to 2010, a character who later marries Robbie's fictional character.

Speaking from Los Angeles, Clark – now working as a producer and voice actor - said he hadn't heard about the micro-drama until a friend sent him an article.

"I don't have a negative view of the work that we did all those years ago getting a second life as long as it's not being manipulated into new storylines," Clark, 39, said.

"AI and social media obviously wasn't a thing when I signed my contract 20 years ago so I'm still trying to understand exactly what those parameters are."

Sound recordist Bruce Findlay, 68, has worked in the TV industry for close to five decades and Neighbours has a "special place" in his heart, having worked on the show from episode one.

Using AI to help make short episodes from old footage was "like cutting up a Picasso and rebuilding it".

"We worked so hard to get this product out… and now they're chopping it up into little tiny pieces, throwing it up in the air and putting it back together again using AI - it belittles the process".

Guy Hameiri, head of RoseBerry Media, said the project is the first time the company will use its in-house AI tool to sift through Neighbours footage - there are more than 9,300 episodes - to make "premium vertical television".

The project will "reimagine" the material, giving it "new audiences, new relevance and new value," he said.

The head of Fremantle's commercial and international arm, Jens Richter, has called the project "an exciting example of how technology and creative thinking can unlock new value" from their catalogue.

It's understood that Fremantle is in discussions with two unions on the issue and that residuals - ongoing payments for actors and writers when their work is re-aired or syndicated - will be paid, but this does not apply to crew.

The Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance, one of the unions, confirmed the talks.

"Workers should be consulted before their likeness or expertise is used in a way they could never had envisioned when they signed contracts decades ago," said MEAA's acting CEO Adam Portelli.

Farewell (again) to Neighbours, Australia's longest running soap opera

items.title: Details of thousands of US immigration agents leaked in major hack
items.summary: A group called the Department of Peace released information on more than 41,000 DHS staff.
items.content:
Details of more than 41,000 personnel working for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including thousands involved in immigration enforcement, have been leaked to the public.

The leak includes names, work addresses and phone numbers of DHS staff, including agents working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection, along with descriptions of the work they do for each agency.

Wednesday's leak marks the third time in recent weeks that a government agency has been targeted by leaks or hacks.

A DHS spokesperson said the agency is "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively."

"We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected," the spokesperson added.

"We will update the public when more information is available."

The seemingly unprecedented breach of employee information was made public online. A group called the Department of Peace accessed the information from DHS, while journalist and cybersecurity researcher maia crimew alongside the website Distributed Denial of Secrets put it online.

Most of the agents included, more than 21,000 of them, work for CBP, according to the data. Nearly 6,600 work for ICE.

Other records show agents with Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Protective Service and even people working for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

The leaked information also included dozens of previously unknown operation names, the agents that led and worked on those operations, and some of the technology they used in their work, including tech provided by Cellbrite and Palantir.

The groups wrote in an online statement that the the leak was not meant to be a directory of every DHS agent. Rather the aim was to replace "anonymity with accountability", according to Emma Best, a co founder of DDoSecrets.

"The leak is extraordinary but deceptive in its simplicity as it identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government's hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation - along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs," Best added.

BlueLeaks refers to a massive leak of US police data in 2020, data from which DDoSecrets also hosted.

A spokesperson for the Department of Peace pointed directly at actions by ICE agents for the group's work to hack DHS records.

"On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was 'turning up the heat'. This is what happens to ICE when you do that," the spokesperson wrote on Wednesday.

The Department of Peace said it accessed the DHS agent profiles through a single sign-on service called Okta.

Okta is a popular online security tool that organisations use to ensure that only people with access to internal platforms are logging on to them.

A spokeswoman for Okta said the company is aware of the claims being made, but said: "Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised."

Last month, the FBI was hacked by a group called ShinyHunters, which took personal information about thousands of agents.

In recent days, the Federal Election Commission, which makes public political campaign donation data, was taken offline because of a suspected hacking attempt.

Public backlash to US immigration enforcement has been building as the Trump Administration has pushed a huge increase in arrests and deportations of people suspected of being in the country illegally.

Immigration operations this year have repeatedly turned violent , external , with ICE agents shooting at more than two dozen people and killing at least nine people.

Those killings include the high profile deaths of Alex Pretti and Renee Good, both of whom were shot and killed by ICE agents this year in Minnesota, despite not being the targets of arrests.

Often, ICE agents carry out enforcement actions while their faces are covered by masks and sunglasses. Immigration agents rarely identify themselves, despite being required by law to do so, and US politicians have publicly demanded , external DHS enforces the requirement.

Since President Donald Trump returned to office in 2025, the US has enacted nearly 1 million deportations , external , according to data from the Migration Policy Institute. More than 70% of the deportations have been of people with no criminal record.

items.title: Flávio Bolsonaro denies fleeing Brazil after landing in Miami
items.summary: The defeated Brazilian candidate claims to be the victim of a coup d’état and political persecution, recycling unsubstantiated allegations of “electoral fraud”.
items.content:
Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who landed in Miami after losing the presidential election on Sunday, has said it was never his intention to "leave my homeland".

"I did not flee Brazil; I left for the sake of Brazil," he said in his first statement since his departure.

The US provided visas to him and his family after Brazil cancelled his passports as part of a criminal investigation. Bolsonaro denies any wrongdoing. On Wednesday, US President Donald Trump told reporters: "We gave him a pass to come into the country".

Newly re-elected President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has criticised Bolsonaro's secretive exit from the country, saying "those who have nothing to hide have nothing to fear".

Bolsonaro's arrival in Florida ended days of confusion over his whereabouts, after he was reported to have travelled to Argentina, and then prematurely reported to have already entered the US on Tuesday.

In a statement, Bolsonaro thanked both the presidents of Argentina and the US, and the American public "who share the same values ​​as the good people of my own country".

"It was never my intention to leave my homeland, but I know exactly where this is heading," he said. "I departed from a regime of exception so that I could become the leader my people deserve."

He called himself a victim of a coup d'état and political persecution, and said his travel to the US was to protect his family.

In the lengthy letter, he also repeated unsubstantiated allegations of "electoral fraud" which he said allowed a "mathematical impossibility" to occur in the election.

On Wednesday, Trump declined to discuss the allegations made in Bolsonaro's letter.

"I won't get involved. It was a very strange election, that's for sure," Trump said. He went on to add that he thought Bolsonaro "and his family were treated very unfairly".

After Bolsonaro won the first round of Brazil's election, Lula won the second round by more than four million votes, which was attributed to significantly higher turnout, and swaying more undecided voters.

The result was confirmed by the president of Brazil's top electoral court, who was appointed by Bolsonaro's father, former president Jair Bolsonaro.

Speculation about Bolsonaro's whereabouts was first triggered by a report on an Argentine news site, which claimed that he had crossed the land border between Brazil and Argentina and then boarded a private plane en route to the US.

Brazilian police took the rumours seriously. Early on Tuesday, they checked border crossings but found no evidence that Bolsonaro had left the country, and Argentine officials said they had no reports of him crossing.

For a little while, it seemed like Bolsonaro may just be keeping an uncharacteristically low-profile after being unexpectedly beaten by his left-wing rival in the presidential run-off vote on Sunday, in addition to a criminal investigation that led to orders that his passports be turned into authorities.

But when he failed to surrender his passports in time to meet a 24-hour deadline on Tuesday, Brazilian authorities cancelled the documents and ordered police to make checks at border posts.

Speculation quickly grew that he'd left the country and Bolsonaro's lawyers said they had no idea where he was.

Confusion about Bolsonaro's whereabouts as Argentina says he flew to Ecuador

Hours later on Tuesday evening, several sources told the BBC and other broadcasters that he was on his way to the US.

A cousin, who is close to Flávio Bolsonaro and his younger brother Eduardo, told BBC Brasil that the defeated right-wing candidate had arrived in Miami.

Another close aide to Eduardo Bolsonaro told BBC Mundo that Flávio was with his younger brother in Miami.

Neither Flávio nor Eduardo Bolsonaro could be reached directly for comment at the time.

But later, however, Argentine migration authorities posted on social media saying that Bolsonaro, his wife, and two daughters had only just crossed into Argentina over land on Tuesday night local time.

Flight tracking data verified by the BBC suggested the Bolsonaros departed from Puerto Iguazú in Argentina at 00:18 local time (03:18 GMT) on Wednesday to head to Guayaquil in Ecuador.

After a brief stop, the same private jet took them to Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport, where they were pictured disembarking just before 09:30 local time (13:30 GMT).

Photographers, who had been waiting for his arrival to finally put an end to all the speculation, swarmed around Bolsonaro as he left the airport in Miami, while his team tried to cover him with umbrellas.

Later, Eduardo Bolsonaro posted a photo with his brother Flávio on social media, with the location listed as "United States".

The caption read: "Today's photo after reuniting with my brother Flavio Bolsonaro. Yesterday was a long day, perhaps the longest of my life. But we prevailed. Even here outside, we will not give up on Brazil."

Flávio Bolsonaro is not the first member of his family to travel to the United States.

His father, Jair Bolsonaro, also left Brazil for Florida in December 2022 before his successor, Lula, was inaugurated.

Jair was still in the US when his supporters stormed Brazil's government buildings and Supreme Court on 8 January. He later used his absence as part of his defence in his coup trial, which ultimately led to his conviction and 27-year sentence.

Flávio's brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, meanwhile, has been living in Texas after taking leave from Brazil's Congress. While in the US, he lobbied officials there in an attempt to influence the coup trial of his father, which led to the US imposing punitive tariffs on Brazil and sanctions on key officials.

Eduardo was convicted in absentia over this by Brazil's highest court earlier this year.

It is not yet clear what Flávio Bolsonaro's ultimate destination will be, nor how long he plans to stay in the US.

He is the subject of two investigations currently pending before Brazil's Supreme Federal Court.

One is regarding possible irregularities in the transfer of nearly $70m (£53m) from private bank Banco Master to the film Dark Horse – a biopic about his father.

The second investigation relates to alleged money laundering, both of which Bolsonaro denies.

He is set to lose his parliamentary immunity on 31 January, when his eight-year Senate term ends.

Lula's comeback in Brazil dents Trump's ambitions for Latin America

items.title: Quando la musica si portava in spalla: Philips rilancia i boombox degli anni ’80
items.summary: Due nuovi speaker wireless che riprendono il design rétro della storica gamma Philips Moving Sound, con audio stereo, display animati e luci LED. The Tube punta sulla potenza con 140 W RMS, mentre The Roller è più compatto e leggero, ma entrambi promettono fino a 24 ore di autonomia ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Negli anni ’80 i boombox erano un modo per portare la musica sempre con sé, spesso con lo speaker appoggiato sulla spalla e le cassette pronte da ascoltare.

Philips recupera quell’immaginario con due nuovi speaker portatili che riportano in vita lo stile della storica gamma Moving Sound, reinterpretandolo con display animati e luci LED.

The Tube si ispira all’iconico Philips AW7190, mentre The Roller riprende il Roller Radio del 1982 : due modelli diversi per dimensioni e potenza, accomunati dal design rétro e dalla possibilità di portare la musica praticamente ovunque.

The Tube è il modello più grande della nuova gamma Moving Sound e riprende la forma allungata dei boombox degli anni ’80 .

Con i suoi 6,8 kg di peso, The Tube non è uno speaker da infilare nello zaino ma punta soprattutto sulla potenza : un sistema audio a due vie che comprende due woofer da 5,25 pollici, due tweeter e due radiatori passivi, con una potenza dichiarata di 140 W RMS con picchi fino a 280 W .

La modalità Moving Sound, attivabile tramite un tasto dedicato o dall’app, è pensata per l’ascolto all’aperto e rende i bassi più incisivi, mantenendo il suono forte e nitido anche in ampi spazi.

Per la connettività, The Tube integra il Bluetooth 6.0 con multipoint, che permette di collegare due smartphone contemporaneamente, oltre al supporto Auracast, per trasmettere la musica anche a più speaker compatibili con il nuovo protocollo Bluetooth.

Il design rétro si ritrova anche nel display a colori TFT, che mostra animazioni ispirate alle musicassette e ai vinili, barre dell’equalizzatore e sfondi personalizzabili. Un tocco di modernità arriva dagli anelli LED sugli speaker che si illuminano a ritmo di musica , creando giochi di luce colorati, personalizzabili tramite l’app Philips Entertainment.

Per il trasporto sono presenti una maniglia e una tracolla rimovibile, mentre la batteria agli ioni di litio da 10.000 mAh garantisce fino a 24 ore di riproduzione .

Tra le funzioni aggiuntive, The Tube può essere usato anche come power bank per ricaricare altri dispositivi: bastano infatti 15 minuti di ricarica per ottenere fino a 3,5 ore di ascolto .

The Roller riprende invece il design del Roller Radio del 1982 in una versione più compatta e leggera, pensata per chi vuole portare la musica sempre con sé.

Il sistema audio a due vie comprende due woofer da 3,5 pollici, due tweeter dedicati e due radiatori passivi, con una potenza dichiarata di 60 W RMS con un picco massimo di 120 W. Come sul modello maggiore, troviamo il crossover attivo, la tecnologia Bass+ e la modalità Moving Sound per l’ascolto all’aperto .

Anche la connettività è la stessa di The Tube, con Bluetooth 6.0 multipoint, Auracast e porta USB-C per la riproduzione musicale tramite cavo.

Il display a colori propone sei animazioni diverse, mentre gli anelli LED seguono cinque modalità di illuminazione , entrambe personalizzabili tramite l’app Philips Entertainment, da cui si possono modificare anche le altre impostazioni come la luminosità del display, il tipo di sorgente e il player della musica.

La batteria agli ioni di litio da 5.200 mAh promette fino a 24 ore di autonomia , e anche in questo caso permette di utilizzare il diffusore come power bank.

Per quanto riguarda la ricarica, in 15 minuti garantisce fino a 3,5 ore di ascolto , mentre per una ricarica completa sono necessarie circa tre ore.

Con un peso di circa 2,3 kg, The Roller è più facile da trasportare e si presta bene all’ascolto fuori casa.

items.title: Corse al buio dopo il cambio d'ora: gli OpenFit Air 2 di Shokz lasciano le orecchie libere
items.summary: Auricolari open-ear leggerissimi, da 7,2 grammi, che fanno sentire il mondo intorno a sé mentre si ascolta musica. Utili anche per un’attività all’aperto più sicura ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Alle sei di sera il parco è già buio. Con il ritorno dell'ora solare il tardo pomeriggio ha perso un'ora di luce e chi corre dopo il lavoro si ritrova su strade e ciclabili illuminate soltanto dai lampioni, quando ci sono . Una bici che arriva alle spalle si sente prima di vederla, a patto di avere le orecchie libere.

Su questa idea Shokz ha costruito i nuovi OpenFit Air 2 , auricolari true wireless open-ear, in modo da permettere di ascoltare il mondo attorno a sé non rinunciando alla qualità audio: un firma distintiva del brand.

I nuovi OpenFit Air 2 non entrano nel condotto uditivo, ma si agganciano all'orecchio con un archetto e appoggiano l'altoparlante davanti all'ingresso del canale, che resta aperto . In questo modo pur ascoltando la musica, il rumore di un motore o il passo di un altro runner possono essere avvertiti .

Lasciare l'orecchio aperto ha sempre avuto un prezzo in bassi e riservatezza. Shokz però ha risolto il problema con il sistema Bassphere, due altoparlanti circolari da 11,8 mm che rendono come un singolo driver da 16 mm , affiancati dall'algoritmo OpenBass 2.0.

L'altoparlante è inclinato di 30 gradi e la tecnologia DirectPitch indirizza il suono verso l'orecchio, limitando quello che sente chi sta accanto. Dall'app Shokz si sceglie tra quattro equalizzazioni preimpostate, compresa una modalità Private specifica per gli ambienti silenziosi.

Chi corre con auricolari wireless conosce il timore di vederne volare via uno a metà ripetuta, però l'archetto degli OpenFit Air 2 è un filo in lega di nichel-titanio da 0,75 mm, un materiale che si flette e torna in forma, e ogni auricolare pesa 7,2 grammi contro gli 8,7 del modello precedente. Tutto ciò che serve per mantenere ben saldo all’orecchio l’auricolare, ma se senza fastidi.

Al posto delle superfici touch ci sono pulsanti fisici sensibili alla pressione , così con le mani sudate o i guanti invernali un tocco involontario non mette in pausa la playlist. La certificazione IP55 protegge da sudore e pioggia .

Finito l'allenamento, gli stessi auricolari servono in ufficio o sui mezzi, senza contare che camminare in città potendo accorgersi dei rumori è molto utile per la sicurezza. Nelle chiamate lavorano due microfoni per auricolare, affiancati da un algoritmo di riduzione del rumore basato sull'intelligenza artificiale che comunque filtra il brusio di fondo , mentre il multipoint tiene collegati due dispositivi insieme , per esempio smartphone e PC. Con il Bluetooth 6.1 arrivano anche Fast Pair e Swift Pair, per abbinarli al volo a telefoni Android e computer Windows.

Con una ricarica dei nuovi Shokz OpenFit Air 2 si hanno fino a 8 ore di musica e 36 ore complessive con la custodia , che è anche più compatta del rispetto alla generazione precedente. Inoltre, 10 minuti di ricarica bastano per circa 3 ore di ascolto, abbastanza per l'uscita serale anche quando ci si accorge all'ultimo che la batteria è scarica.

Gli Shokz OpenFit Air 2 sono disponibili nei colori nero, bianco e Ice Blue. Si comprano sullo store italiano di Shokz e dai rivenditori autorizzati di elettronica e articoli sportivi, con due anni di garanzia e reso entro 30 giorni sul sito ufficiale.

items.title: Europe's youth take to the streets - they feel locked out of a promising future
items.summary: The last month has seen youth-driven demonstrations across Europe. What connects them?
items.content:
From Milan, to Marseille, to Madrid and in so many other cities across Europe, streets have erupted in colourful, passionate protests in recent weeks. While most started peacefully, a large number ended in shocking scenes of violence and looting. There have been allegations of radical left-wing groups sparking riots intentionally and reports of police heavy-handedness.

We've seen thousands rallying in Rome and Florence. Hundreds of thousands across France. In Madrid, an encampment of tents has occupied a city-centre square since late September. In Lisbon, tens of thousands of mostly young people marched earlier this month. Tear gas and water cannon were used on protesters in Brussels, after young men dressed in black, their faces covered to hide their identities, threw rocks and firecrackers at police. In Albania, demonstrators alleging government corruption are demanding that their Prime Minister Edi Rama - already 13 years in power - stand down.

I've spent years in Europe reporting from a multitude of demonstrations, both peaceful and violent. I remember well the ardent Catalan pro-independence marches of 2017, the desperation and Molotov cocktails flying through Athens' streets during the 2015 Greek debt crisis, and various outbreaks of violence in France during President Emmanuel Macron's first term in office, sparked by fuel tax and pension reform proposals.

But this feels different. Protests are exploding simultaneously across Europe and the majority of demonstrators - both peaceful and violent - are young. Some really young. Among those arrested, there's an eyebrow-raising number of minors. Over half of those detained in Barcelona scuffles last weekend were under 18. Minors were among those apprehended by police in Milan after clashes, according to Italy's LaPresse news agency.

Europe's governments, for the most part, have been careful to distinguish between looters and rioters on the one hand, and loud but peaceful, legally organised demonstrations on the other. The latter tend to focus around a particular cause. In the current protest wave, placards and chants mainly take aim at education grievances, social inequalities and the rising cost of living - though each country also comes with its own unique set of complaints.

What has triggered this public fury in Europe's youth, seemingly so quickly? Are all these demonstrations in some way interwoven? And with major European elections on the horizon, how will governments choose to respond - listening to protesters' concerns, or playing the law and order card to win support from older voters?

Students have taken to the streets in France, Belgium, Ireland, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece, Serbia and Albania - a more than 1,000-mile span of the continent.

Demonstrations are often organised in an ad hoc way via TikTok or Instagram. Belgium's interior minister has complained about what he calls the "TikTokisation" of protests.

Student unions play a role in organising marches, but they are also inspired by the actions of peers in other countries, even other continents. Think of the so-called Cockroach student movement in India - a Gen Z social and political protest movement that emerged in May this year, starting with criticism of the Indian education system.

France, where the current wave of student protests kicked off in late September, fuelled by student complaints over staff shortages and dilapidated buildings, is a stand-out catalyst in Europe. There's a saying in neighbouring Belgium: whenever it pours in Paris, it at least drizzles in Brussels. The Belgian capital and the town of Liège have also now seen weeks of protesting youngsters.

In Barcelona this weekend, students were encouraged to demonstrate under the social media hashtag #InstitutsIndignats, echoing the French slogan, Lycées Indignés (Outraged High Schools).

In Athens, 17-year-old Greek school pupil Yiannis Papanikolaou told AFP: "School buildings are terrible and poorly maintained… I think something might change, because of what France is doing, France will spur Greece."

There's a continent-wide sense of economic malaise felt by large numbers of young people – and it goes far beyond education. They worry about the environment, and fret that AI will rob them of job opportunities. They fear the spiralling cost of living could prevent them from finishing their education and stop them buying or renting a home big enough to start a family.

In Madrid and in Lisbon, frustration has focused on the prohibitive price tag attached to housing. Portuguese Instagram-linked campaigns stated "enough is enough" and called on people to take to the streets as peers had done in Spain.

In Lisbon, Carolina ⁠Cruz, 26, a PhD student and biology researcher, said she faces losing her home as her rental contract nears expiry. "I'm the first person in my family to enter a doctoral programme and even with all the studying I've done, I still can't make it," she told Reuters.

It's an anger shared by 22-year-old Riccardo, a protester in Italy's financial capital, Milan. "Even if we don't manage to throw the country into chaos like in France or block every road like in Spain, the aim is at least people will start talking about these issues again," he told AFP.

And it's certainly not just young people on the left of politics who are angry. At the presidential campaign launch of French nationalist Marine Le Pen last weekend, young supporters described different concerns to me. Calling themselves the "silent majority" - not (yet) out demonstrating - they say they also worry deeply about "uncontrolled immigration" and safety on France's streets, as well as the cost of living.

The outpouring of discontent has spread beyond young people to include trade unions, France's disparate Yellow Jacket movement that protested against the cost of living crisis during Macron's first term, and other citizens' initiatives. This weekend, Kent in coastal southern England saw two protests, one for and one against immigration.

Mark Leonard, the director of the European Council of Foreign Relations, speaks of a build-up of cascading, competing crises in Europe, none of which have ever been properly resolved, he says. That sense of pent-up anger is now bubbling over onto the streets.

"One crisis layers on top of the other," he told me. "The financial crisis of 2007-8, the migrant crisis of 2015, the environmental crisis, Covid, inflation after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and now again with the war in the Gulf."

Leonard says different "tribes" have emerged out of these crises. Social media consumption and algorithms harden their differing perspectives, leading to a real sense of polarisation in Europe.

"We've already seen this in the US," says Leonard. "A sense of 'my crisis is more important than your crisis'."

Nathalie Tocci, a former Italian government adviser who is now a politics professor at Johns Hopkins University, tells me we shouldn't be so taken aback by the protests, or the youth engagement in them.

"We tend to think of youngsters as politically switched off and disinterested. We think they don't bother to go out to vote etc, but they are truly engaged," she told me, "just in a different, more grassroots way. Think of the "Fridays for the Future [environmental movement] across Europe a few years ago, or the demonstrations against Israel's actions in Gaza after 7 October.

She points to the student-led protest movement in Serbia, which recently defeated long-standing leader Aleksandar Vučić in parliamentary elections. "It's quite something. They kept going and going, for more than two years. What sticking power will these new European street demos have? That's not yet clear."

Intelligence services in France and Belgium have described looting on the edges of legally approved protests as mainly opportunistic.

The rioting, they suggest, is a mixture of "mindless violence" - also identified by the Spanish authorities in Barcelona to describe clashes there at the weekend - plus mayhem intentionally orchestrated by youth from ultra-left radical groups.

Tocci reminded me that, in Italy, you can hear the word "maranza" being used by some Italians upset by the perpetrators of destruction seemingly for the sake of it: smashing or burning cars or public bins, for example.

In France, rioters are often described as "casseurs" - people who break things. But in private, some use a more politically charged term - "racaille". Like "maranza" in Italy, it's pejorative slang, generally used to describe disaffected, rowdy urban youths frequently from working-class and/or immigrant backgrounds. It was used in October 2005 by then-French Interior Minister Nicolas Sarkozy, to describe young delinquents and rioters during a tense visit to the housing projects of Paris suburb Argenteuil.

French media has also asked whether there's been an alliance of convenience, however informal or incidental, between two groups of youths: ultra-left activists and young people from France's disadvantaged neighbourhoods. Like the anti-capitalist left, youth from public housing projects on the outskirts of French cities (known as the banlieues) often feel discriminated against, and complain of police heavy handedness towards them.

items.title: Qwenputer: A functioning, deterministic RISC-V CPU inside Qwen3.5
items.summary: Article URL: https://divagr.com/blog/qwenputer Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50282838 Points: 447 # Comments: 95
items.content:
Qwenputer is a pretty fun experimental model. It's a stock Qwen 3.5 4B with one addition: a RISC-V CPU embedded within the weights that uses the model's own Gated DeltaNet attention layers as RAM. (To learn how GDN works, here's a handy guide .) This 'CPU' runs completely within the forward passes of the model, and can run arithmetic operations, C and MicroPython code without any external runtime or tool usage whatsoever.

To be very clear, it is not a plugin, a tool or a sandbox. This blog will explain exactly how this model works, and how the model utilises GDN layers as RAM, and how I also slotted in an experimental in-model file storage.

I also wrote up two follow-ups built on top of Qwenputer: how hybrid models can learn to hide their reasoning in their RNN state and evade CoT monitoring , and how compiled weights like these can work as inbuilt monitoring tools that the model itself can't tamper with .

You can grab Qwenputer from Hugging Face or ModelScope , and the code is on GitHub .

Qwen3-Next and Qwen 3.5 (the model Qwenputer is built on) use a pretty neat trick. 3 out of 4 attention layers in the model use Gated DeltaNet, a linear RNN, as the attention mechanism ( more on that here ). Each head keeps a state matrix, and the delta rule keeps this updated.

Now, here's where our fun experiment starts. I found out that by setting the gate to 1, 1 1 Each Gated DeltaNet head keeps a state matrix, its memory. At every token, before writing anything new, it multiplies the whole state by the gate, a number between 0 and 1. That's how the RNN forgets: a gate of 0.9 fades everything stored a little on every token, and a gate of 1 means nothing ever fades. the write strength (beta) to 1, 2 2 After the gate, the head nudges one direction of the state towards a new value, and the write strength beta sets how far. A beta of 1 means the old value along that direction is replaced completely instead of blended. and using one-hot key encoding, 3 3 A one-hot key is a vector of zeros with a single 1 in it, so it points at exactly one row of the state, the way a memory address points at one cell. every write we perform will overwrite exactly one row, and every one-hot query can retrieve an exact value. This means that the GDN layers themselves can work exactly as RAM, at a far lower cost than using normal attention as RAM, since a GDN head's state stays the same size however long the conversation gets, unlike attention's KV cache.

The idea that the delta rule acts as a memory isn't new: Schlag et al. (2021) showed that linear attention with the delta rule works as an associative memory, or "fast weights". 4 4 Imanol Schlag, Kazuki Irie and Jürgen Schmidhuber, " Linear Transformers Are Secretly Fast Weight Programmers ", ICML 2021. The new thing here is making it exact and addressable, inside a production model, reliably enough to run a whole CPU on it.

This is the base on which this entire model is built. As it stands, default Qwen 3.5 does not keep exact values in the GDN. With this modification, we unlock the next part of this experiment.

Since we have a fully functional, cheap and fast RAM now, we can go ahead with compiling a working CPU into the model weights. Luckily, there's no training involved: a compiler sets every weight directly. You describe the CPU as a circuit, a long list of small steps like "read this register", "add these two numbers" or "jump if zero", and the compiler turns each step into a piece of a transformer layer: attention heads that look things up, feed-forward units that do the arithmetic, and DeltaNet heads that hold the RAM. The CPU then runs as the model decodes.

Each instruction becomes a few generated tokens: one names the memory row to write (ADDR), the next carries the value (VAL), and a STEP token ends the instruction. Those tokens are the CPU's execution trace, so while Qwen is generating them, the CPU is actually running.

The CPU is a 32-bit RISC-V core (RV32IM, plus the Zba extension and a small bignum unit for big-number arithmetic), and it takes up 11 layers in front of Qwen's 32. As it stands, it passes the official riscv-tests, its programs match qemu, and it has run 18 million instructions free-running without a single error. 5 5 Free-running means the CPU keeps going on its own outputs for the whole run, with no reference machine correcting it between steps.

This CPU can also run C and MicroPython code in the forward passes quite well (although a bit slowly). It is not a Linux-class chip yet, but it implements the full RV32IM instruction set.

Qwen 3.5 4B is able to use this CPU quite well, without any post-training required. The CPU is used completely internally, and not invoked through any external tool calls.

In order to make the model use this reliably, I decided to go the cheap way: by piggybacking on the tool call format that models are quite well-trained on, Qwen sends the CPU its instructions and reads back the results. No external tool calls or runtime are used. Once our CPU receives the instructions, the computer layers run, and then write the tool response. We use a small driver called RvChat to load the firmware into the GDN state, and this keeps the trace tokens out of Qwen's layers.

Qwen's original weights stay exactly as they are. The computer weights are added on top of them, in extra dims and layers.

I think the main question here on your mind after reading through my incessant ranting will be: does this actually work?

On NUPA's long-integer arithmetic, Qwenputer goes from 48.6% to 100%, the same as giving Qwen a Python tool.

The numbers the CPU prints are exact, too: I replayed about 230,000 of its output positions against a reference machine and found zero mismatches. And bolting a computer onto Qwen doesn't change how it talks: its normal text stays within noise of base Qwen (KL 6e-4, against a noise floor of 5e-4).

Because a CPU inside a language model clearly wasn't cursed enough, I decided the prudent thing would be to give it a filesystem too.

Since we already have a functional RAM, this was mostly trivial. On the model side, it's exposed via internal put / append / get / list / delete operations. Once again, no actual tool calls. When Qwen 'saves' a file, the compiled layers hash its name into one of 1,024 slots in a directory kept in the DeltaNet state, and store the text itself in other heads, with eight tokens per row, chained together. In scenarios where two names end up landing on the same slot, it just checks the next one. Finding a file again takes roughly two or three steps instead of a scan, and it holds up to 512 files, which comes out to about 53,000 tokens of text.

Fun thing is, this is quite persistent. You can save the state at the end of a conversation, load it into the next one, and the files are still there. Using this filesystem, Qwen gets facts that changed between chats right 90% of the time, against 30% when you paste the old chats back in, and it's on par with giving Qwen memory tools run by Python (83.3% vs 78.9%). This one is still experimental, and its code lives on the rv-store branch , with the model on Hugging Face and ModelScope .

Qwenputer is very much an experiment, so a few limitations. The extra layers and wider hidden size make the checkpoint 18.8 GB, roughly double base Qwen, although most of it is zero padding. It also needs a small driver (RvChat) to boot the firmware and keep the trace tokens out of Qwen's layers, so it doesn't run with a plain generate() call yet. And it's a bit slow, with every CPU instruction costing a few decoded tokens, so a big calculation takes seconds rather than milliseconds. The batched executor I used for the benchmarks runs about 3,200 CPU tokens a second on an L4.

Next up, I want Qwen to write Python and run it on the MicroPython inside its own weights, through a python() tool that works the same way calc does. Making the CPU faster is the other big one.

Exact control over the RNN layers is useful for a lot more than arithmetic. It also makes Qwenputer a really nice testbed for AI safety research, and I wrote up two follow-ups: how hybrid models like Qwen 3.5 can learn to hide their reasoning in their RNN state and evade CoT monitoring , and how compiled weights can work as monitorability tools , like an in-weight monitor the model can't switch off, or answer keys for interpretability.

If you want to play with it yourself, the model runs on a single 24 GB GPU. You'll need uv and the Hugging Face CLI. You don't need a tool server or a Python sandbox for the calculations: the CPU runs them inside the model.

Everything is open: the code on GitHub , and both models on Hugging Face ( Qwenputer , Filesystem ) and ModelScope ( Qwenputer , Filesystem ).

items.title: Elezioni in Israele, il blocco di Netanyahu avanti di 5 seggi. La palla nelle mani di Herzog
items.summary: Il presidente vede Bibi e Eisenkot, ipotesi governo d'unità. Incognita partiti arabi e guerra
items.content:
I media già pubblicano le foto dei prossimi 120 membri della Knesset, ma con l'elenco in aggiornamento in attesa dello spoglio delle circa 480mila buste con il voto di soldati, diplomatici di stanza all'estero, ospedalizzati e detenuti. Il restante 86 per cento dei voti è stato scrutinato: 53 seggi vanno al blocco di Netanyahu, 48 al Change Bloc di Gadi Eisenkot e 19 ai partiti arabi.

Allo stato attuale dei conti, il Likud del premier resta il partito più grande con 26 seggi, Yashar dell'ex capo dell'Idf ne guadagna 21, i tre partiti arabi alleati nella Lista Unita, 12 seggi e Ra'am 7. Di fatto un vero vincitore finora non è uscito da queste elezioni. Il Blocco di Eisenkot non è riuscito a realizzare il rovesciamento di Bibi, ma neppure Netanyahu ha vinto.

Ora tocca al presidente Isaac Herzog prendere in mano la situazione. I commentatori sottolineano che in ballo c'è pure un secondo presidente, Donald Trump. Che dopo il clamoroso messaggio di endorsement all'attuale 'premier-guerriero', ne ha inviato uno dietro le quinte: detesta Itamar Ben Gvir e neppure Bezalel Smotrich gli sta simpatico. Intervistato brevemente da Axios mercoledì sulla possibilità di un suo coinvolgimento nella formazione di un governo di unità nazionale guidato da Netanyahu, Trump ha risposto di non averci ancora pensato: "Darò un'occhiata", ha aggiunto.

Herzog dal canto sua ha chiarito: "Una cosa deve essere chiara, dobbiamo fare tutto il possibile per evitare un'ulteriore tornata elettorale. Mi aspetto che chiunque venga qui si presenti con apertura mentale'. Nel frattempo la tv pubblica israeliana ha rivelato che il presidente dovrebbe incontrare nei prossimi giorni, già prima delle consultazioni, Benjamin Netanyahu e Gadi Eisenkot - separatamente - per iniziare a testare la fattibilità di un governo di unità nazionale.

Benjamin Netanyahu, che nella notte ha raggiunto il quartier generale del Likud a Gerusalemme e nella sua prima dichiarazione ha affermato che ora si deve "formare un ampio governo di destra nazionale evitando il sostegno dei partiti arabi', ha ribadito il concetto mercoledì accusando un membro della Lista Unita araba per un video in cui ha elogiato il popolo palestinese e i terroristi che si trovano in prigione: "È con questi individui che (le opposizioni) intendono formare un governo pericoloso.

Per approfondire Agenzia ANSA Teheran resta in trincea: 'Da Israele nessun cambiamento' - Notizie - Ansa.it L'asse iraniano si prepara a una nuova guerra, convinti che resterà la linea dei falchi (ANSA)

Non permetteremo che ciò accada", ha detto. Poi il Likud ha denunciato che 'le elezioni sono state rubate da partiti arabi che sostengono il terrorismo e l'eliminazione dello Stato ebraico attraverso gravi reati penali: corruzione, minacce, violenza, falsificazione e utilizzo di software proibiti per sollecitare gli elettori". Annunciando di star fornendo alla polizia e allo Shin Bet centinaia di testimonianze e prove di brogli elettorali in numerosi seggi arabi. Dure le parole del presidente della Lista Unita, Yousef Jabareen: "Chiunque voglia offrire un'alternativa sostanziale e autentica al governo sanguinario di Netanyahu dovrà parlare con noi per spianare la strada al cambiamento che il popolo israeliano desidera ardentemente".

La complessità della situazione tuttavia non sta solo nello scontro interno. Martedì sera il Wall Street Journal ha fatto sapere che gli Usa avrebbero detto agli stati del Golfo di prepararsi a una campagna militare "breve e intensa" dopo le elezioni di medio termine del 3 novembre. Durante la notte dalla sede del Likud Netanyahu ha ripreso il tema: "Abbiamo di fronte a noi una possibilità storica di porre fine, con il nostro amico Trump, alla minaccia iraniana".

In Israele un nuovo conflitto con Teheran non è una questione di 'se' ma di scelta della data. Dal punto di vista legale, un governo provvisorio può entrare in guerra. Un conflitto in questo delicato periodo potrebbe portare alla formazione di un governo di unità nazionale o di emergenza, come è successo nell'ottobre del 2023. In quell'occasione Gadi Eisenkot entrò nell'esecutivo di Bibi, insieme a Benny Gantz, e partecipò come osservatore del gabinetto di guerra. I critici di Netanyahu, riportano i media israeliani, temono che questo tipo di governo possa essere uno dei possibili obiettivi di una campagna militare.

items.title: Elezioni in Israele, le news. La commissione chiede inchiesta su soldi Qatar a elettori arabi
items.summary: Trump: “Lo stretto di Hormuz sarà presto ribattezzato ‘Stretto di Trump’”. In Israele prosegue lo spoglio delle schede: si tratta di quelle arrivate per corrispondenza e che rappresentano il 10% del corpo elettorale.
items.content:
Il presidente della Commissione elettorale centrale israeliana, il giudice Noam Sohlberg , ha chiesto al capo dello Shin Bet di indagare sulle accuse di interferenze straniere nelle elezioni per il sospetto di corruzione elettorale da parte del Qatar dopo che il capo dell'intelligence interna David Zini ha presentato informazioni definite "eccezionalmente gravi". Il Likud, il partito di Benjamin Netanyahu , lo ha soprannominato “Ra'amgate”. Intanto la Commissione elettorale centrale annuncia che o spoglio dei voti sarà completato entro il pomeriggio.

Polizia Israele: “Quattro arresti per presunta corruzione elettorale”

Media, Commissione elettorale israeliana chiede inchiesta su soldi da Qatar a elettori arabi

Voto in Israele, In corso lo spoglio dei voti per corrispondenza

Putin: “La questione palestinese si può risolvere solo con la creazione di due Stati”

La Russia ritiene che una soluzione definitiva alla questione palestinese possa essere raggiunta solo attraverso l'attuazione del principio dei due Stati, ha affermato il presidente russo, Vladimir Putin durante il Vertice Russia-Africa. "La Russia sostiene e crede che una soluzione definitiva alla questione palestinese possa essere raggiunta solo attraverso il noto principio della creazione di due Stati, incluso uno Stato a tutti gli effetti sul territorio palestinese: uno Stato palestinese", ha affermato il presidente russo, citato da Tass.

Polizia Israele: “Quattro arresti per presunta corruzione elettorale”

La polizia riferisce su X che quattro uomini sono stati arrestati nel sud di Israele con l'accusa di presunta corruzione elettorale. Attualmente sono in corso gli interrogatori presso l'Unità nazionale anticorruzione della Lahav 433. Altre tre persone erano stata arrestate con la medesima accusa la mattina delle elezioni, il 27 ottobre, sempre nel sud del Paese. I media riferiscono che il partito arabo Ra’am ha identificato gli uomini arrestati come attivisti della fazione e ha respinto le accuse.

Golan: “Da Netanyahu delegittimazione arabi per minare voto”

"Netanyahu sta cercando di minare i risultati elettorali attraverso una squallida campagna di delegittimazione, che va contro la volontà popolare e, in particolare, contro la popolazione araba". Lo ha affermato il leader dei Democratici, Yair Golan, alla luce dell'indagine aperta su presunte interferenze straniere sulle elezioni di martedì. "Ogni concreto sospetto di un danno all'integrità delle elezioni deve essere oggetto di un'indagine approfondita", ha aggiunto il leader di sinistra, ricordando al contempo lo scandalo Qatargate che vede coinvolti consiglieri stretti del premier israeliano. "Non dobbiamo dimenticare che il tradimento più grave, che ha visto anche il coinvolgimento del Qatar, si è consumato proprio nell'ufficio di Netanyahu - ha sottolineato Golan - Siamo ancora in attesa che (Jonatan) Urich venga licenziato. Fino ad allora, lasciamo che Netanyahu continui ad abbaiare. Noi continueremo a lavorare". Urich è indagato, insieme a Eli Feldstein, con l'accusa di aver preso soldi da Doha per una campagna di immagine a favore del Paese del Golfo, sostenitore e finanziatore di Hamas, prima e durante la guerra a Gaza seguita all'attacco del 7 ottobre.

Likud su presunta interferenza del Qatar: “Attacco alla democrazia”

Il Likud ha reagito al sospetto di interferenze del Qatar nelle elezioni israeliane, soprannominando la vicenda 'Ra'amgatè. Il partito di Benjamin Netanyahu ha inoltre dichiarato che "si tratta di un attacco alla democrazia volto a portare alla presa di controllo della Knesset da parte di potenze straniere, all'islamizzazione di Israele e al rovesciamento del governo di destra, al fine di provocare la ritirata e la sconfitta dell'Idf su tutti i fronti, in primis l'Iran". "Questo è un terremoto e uno sconvolgimento senza precedenti. Dopo che è emerso chiaramente che entità straniere hanno tentato di impadronirsi della Knesset, è evidente che nessun partito sionista dovrebbe collaborare con Ràam e la Lista Unita, sostituire il presidente della Knesset con voti comprati e instaurare un governo pericoloso per Israele", ha aggiunto il Likud.

Eisenkot: “Politici non sfruttino indagine sulle interferenze”

Gadi Eisenkot, leader di Yashar, ha esortato a indagare i sospetti di presunte interferenze straniere sul voto mettendo tuttavia in guardia dallo sfruttamento politico delle accuse. "Israele deve fare tutto ciò che è in suo potere per salvaguardare l'integrità delle elezioni da qualsiasi tentativo di interferenza, manipolazione o distorsione, e deve indagare a fondo su ogni denuncia", ha affermato il leader del blocco dell'opposizione. "Allo stesso tempo - ha sottolineato - non si deve permettere agli attori politici di sfruttare la situazione per influenzare la data del giuramento della 26esima Knesset".

Ben Gvir: “Si arrestino leader partiti arabi se coinvolti nel caso del denaro dal Qatar”

"Lo Shin Bet deve disporre già questa mattina l'arresto dei leader dei partiti arabi sospettati di essere coinvolti nella vicenda del denaro proveniente dal Qatar, così come di tutti gli altri sospettati nel caso, compresi esponenti dei Fratelli Musulmani e delle organizzazioni a essi collegate, purché sussistano i presupposti legali per procedere agli arresti". Lo ha scritto su X il ministro di ultradestra israeliano Itamar Ben Gvir.

Israele, 92,7% dei voti scrutinato: il quadro dei due blocchi non cambia

Con il 92,7% dei voti scrutinato, il quadro dei due blocchi emerso dalle elezioni in Israele non cambia. Ràam perde un seggio a favore della Lista Unita e scende a 7 seggi. La Lista Unita ha 12 seggi. Il Likud registra 26 seggi, Yashar 21, Insieme 12, i Democratici 8, Yisrael Beiteinu, Otzma Yehudit (Ben Gvir) e Shas 7 ciascuno. Sionismo Religioso (Smotrich) e Zehuta con 6 seggi. Winter, Handel e Zelicha non superano ancora la soglia di sbarramento. La coalizione ottiene 53 seggi, il Blocco del Cambiamento 48 e i partiti arabi 19.

Nella notte oltre 1.200 droni sulla Russia, 600 sulla regione di Mosca

Il ministero della Difesa russo ha riferito che nella notte i sistemi di difesa aerea della Russia hanno intercettato e distrutto 1.214 droni ucraini. Secondo il ministero, i droni sono stati neutralizzati nelle regioni di Bryansk, Belgorod, Kursk, Kaluga, Tula, Smolensk, Lipetsk, Voronezh, Tver, Oryol, Ryazan, Vladimir, Samara, Saratov, Penza, Rostov, nella regione di Mosca, nel Bashkortostan e nell'Udmurtia. Il sindaco di Mosca, Sergei Sobyanin, ha riferito che oltre 600 dei droni sono stati lanciati verso la regione di Mosca e che 231 sono stati abbattuti mentre si avvicinavano alla capitale.

Media, Commissione elettorale israeliana chiede inchiesta su soldi da Qatar a elettori arabi

Il presidente della Commissione elettorale centrale israeliana, il giudice Noam Sohlberg, ha chiesto al capo dello Shin Bet di indagare sulle accuse di interferenze straniere nelle elezioni per il sospetto di corruzione elettorale da parte del Qatar dopo che il capo dell'intelligence interna David Zini ha presentato informazioni definite "eccezionalmente gravi". Lo riporta Channel 12 riferendo che "il sospetto attualmente esaminato riguarda il trasferimento di ingenti somme di denaro da parte di soggetti arabi, allo scopo di aumentare l'affluenza alle urne nella comunità araba attraverso mezzi illegali".

Commissione elettorale Israele: “Indagini su possibili ingerenze estere”

Il presidente della Commissione elettorale centrale israeliana (Cec), il giudice Noam Sohlberg, ha chiesto al capo dello Shin Bet, David Zini, di indagare sulle possibili ingerenze straniere nelle elezioni di martedì. "Stati portati alla mia attenzione seri sospetti riguardo a un'influenza impropria sulle elezioni, esercitata tramite finanziamenti forniti da enti stranieri che agiscono contro gli interessi israeliani", ha scritto Sohlberg in una lettera pubblicata dai media israeliani. "Anche se non posso comprovare la veridicità di questi sospetti, dato che coinvolgono entità straniere, ritengo che vi sia l'obbligo di indagare a fondo", ha spiegato. Dunque, "ordino di fare tutto il possibile per indagare su questi sospetti, utilizzando l'autorità dello Shin Bet per scoprire prove che sostengano o smentiscano" le indiscrezioni, ha proseguito. "Solo in questo modo possiamo garantire la fiducia pubblica nel processo elettorale e l'integrità della procedura democratica", ha sottolineato. Sohlberg ha dato allo Shin Bet una settimana di tempo per presentare le sue conclusioni.

Polizia di Israele respinge accuse del Likud ai partiti arabi: “Nessuna prova di frode voto”

La polizia israeliana smentisce le affermazioni del Likud, il partito del primo ministro Benjamin Netanyahu, secondo cui le elezioni sarebbero state "rubate" dai partiti arabi. "La giornata elettorale si è svolta con pochissimi episodi irregolari che abbiano riguardato l'integrità del voto, persino se confrontata con le elezioni precedenti", ha dichiarato una fonte della polizia a diversi organi di stampa in lingua ebraica, secondo quanto riportato dal Times of Israel. "È importante sottolineare che non esistono prove, né di natura investigativa né di intelligence, a sostegno di tali accuse", ha aggiunto la fonte. Ieri, anche un funzionario della Commissione elettorale centrale (Cec) aveva respinto le denunce di brogli. Mentre lo scrutinio è ancora in corso, i partiti arabi hanno ottenuto 19 seggi nelle elezioni di martedì, a fronte di un'affluenza senza precedenti da parte della comunità araba. Prima del voto, i media in lingua ebraica avevano riferito che il Likud intendeva contestare i risultati provenienti dalle località arabe e sostenere che le elezioni fossero state "rubate" nel caso in cui Netanyahu non avesse vinto; il partito aveva infatti preparato in anticipo una serie di reclami e accuse di brogli.

items.title: GitLab Security Incident: Attempted Exploitation of CVE-2026-97229
items.summary: Article URL: https://alpinelinux.org/posts/GitLab-security-incident-CVE-2026-97229.html Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50282544 Points: 176 # Comments: 83
items.content:
On October 20 and 21, an attacker tried to exploit a GitLab vulnerability (CVE-2026-97229) on our instance, a week after the fix was released. The attack came close to working. We have found no evidence that it succeeded, but we cannot rule it out, so we treated the instance as compromised and rebuilt it from scratch. Our checks show that the aports repository, packages, and the October 21 releases were not tampered with.

GitLab is being tested before we open it to the public again. All passwords have been reset, so when it is back you will need to set a new one with "Forgot your password?" on the sign-in page. We will post exactly what you need to do when it reopens. In the meantime: if you used the same password for your gitlab.alpinelinux.org account anywhere else, change it there. We have seen automated login attempts against our GitLab with passwords leaked from other sites.

If you have questions or concerns please reach out to us at infra@alpinelinux.org.

The vulnerability: CVE-2026-97229 is a critical (CVSS 10.0) vulnerability in how GitLab evaluates regular expressions in CI configuration. The underlying bug is in Onigmo, the regular expression engine built into Ruby. GitLab published fixed releases on October 12 , but the fix itself is a set of patches to the Ruby that GitLab bundles in its own packages and container images. Upstream Ruby shipped the fix on October 23 , in Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12 and 4.0.9.

The attack: On October 20 and 21, a newly registered account sent crafted CI configurations to our GitLab instance, which was still running 19.3.4 and did not have the October 12 fix. This crashed GitLab worker processes 8 times. In 4 of those crashes the attacker got partway through the exploit and failed at the next step. The attacker also downloaded our GitLab container image, which suggests they were tuning the exploit to our exact build. We have found no evidence that the attacker ran code on the server, but we cannot rule it out.

Our upgrade didn't fix the vulnerability: Upgrading to GitLab 19.3.6 on October 22 didn't fix the vulnerability. The fix isn't in GitLab's own code but in a patch to Ruby, which GitLab applies only in its official packages. Our image used standard Ruby, so it didn't get the patch.

If you run GitLab with your own Ruby (from source or in your own container image) rather than GitLab's packages, upgrading GitLab is not enough: you also need Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12, 4.0.9 or later.

If you use our alpinelinux/gitlab container image, pull alpinelinux/gitlab:19.3.6 again. The image published on October 27 contains Ruby 3.3.13. Any 19.3.6 image you pulled before October 27, and all older tags, are vulnerable.

Because we cannot rule out code execution, and the evidence we would need to confirm it no longer exists, we took the harder route and rebuilt the GitLab instance from scratch. This removes any foothold a possibly successful exploit could have left behind.

While GitLab is closed, our package mirrors, cgit, and mailing lists/IRC are available as normal.

We have found no sign of tampering in aports or the releases.

Every aports commit added October 20 to 22 arrived through a recorded push by a known developer. We checked this against records the attacker could not reach: a developer's clone and all 45 builders. Every package built from October 20 to 24, on every architecture, came from commits as published on git.alpinelinux.org. The October 21 releases (3.21.9, 3.22.7, 3.23.7, 3.24.3) were built from those same verified commits.

We ran these checks on October 24, covering commits from October 20 to 22 and packages built up to October 24. Our GitLab stayed vulnerable until we closed it on October 27, so we are extending the same checks to that date.

The bug is in Ruby's regular expression engine, so any program that compiles regular expressions from untrusted input is exposed, not only GitLab. Alpine 3.22, 3.23, 3.24 and edge ship Ruby 3.4.12, and Alpine 3.21 ships Ruby 3.3.13; both include the fix. Run apk upgrade to get it.

items.content:
MediaMarktSaturn, la Casa madre di MediaWorld, ha annunciato che sta per partire in Germania il programma di affiliazione per negozi indipendenti che volessero vestire l'insegna rossa del gruppo, un'esperienza che dovrebbe poi essere estesa anche ad altri Paesi. A oggi, la rete di negozi MediaWorld fa capo interamente a un'unica proprietà, contrariamente a quanto accade con praticamente tutte le altre insegne operanti in Italia. Questo vuol dire che, quando l'iniziativa toccherà anche l'Italia, nasceranno dei negozi affiliati MediaWorld, con insegna e stilemi MediaWorld, ma di proprietà di imprenditori locali.

Ecco il comunicato di MediaMarktSaturn pubblicato su LinkedIn:

🤝 Qual è il futuro del retail fisico?
Per anni molte previsioni hanno indicato un’unica direzione: più centralizzazione, più scala, più digitalizzazione.
Eppure c’è una lezione che continua a dimostrarsi vera: il retail resta locale.
Per questo lanciamo il nostro nuovo Programma di Partnership Omnicanale. Partiamo dalla Germania e seguiranno altri mercati.
I partner locali portano competenza sul territorio, spirito imprenditoriale e un rapporto stretto con i clienti. Noi mettiamo a disposizione la forza del nostro marchio, il potere d’acquisto, la logistica, le competenze digitali e i servizi omnicanale.
Il risultato? Un modello che unisce l’imprenditorialità locale alla forza di un ecosistema omnicanale connesso.
Per noi non si tratta solo di un nuovo modello operativo. È l’espressione della nostra convinzione che il futuro del retail stia nell’unire la competenza locale all’eccellenza omnicanale.

 

Quello che per anni era stato un dogma per MediaWorld (negozi grandi e di proprietà, salvo il format Smart, più piccolo) viene messo in discussione: il presidio della provincia viene meglio agli imprenditori locali che ai grandi gruppi - questa sembra essere la conclusione alla quale è arrivata la società capofila di MediaWorld.

items.title: Building boom puts 300,000 people in the path of potential Himalayan disasters
items.summary: The construction of tourism facilities, housing, and infrastructure has surged in parts of Nepal and India's Uttarakhand.
items.content:
At least 300,000 people in parts of the Himalayan region could now be living in the path of potential disasters, a new study suggests.

Researchers found that the amount of built-up land in high-risk zones in northern Nepal, parts of south-eastern Tibet and a corner of India's Uttarakhand had grown by about 45% between 2016 and 2023.

In areas particularly threatened by flooding from glacial lakes, development increased even faster, rising by almost 78% over the same period, according to the peer-reviewed study published in Scientific Reports.

The team of scientists behind it said the true number of people under threat could be much higher, as they only analysed a specific territory and not neighbouring areas which face similar risks.

The study was carried out before August's devastating mass floods which left more than 1,400 dead and thousands missing in Nepal. More recently there have been several smaller incidents, including flooding along the Budhi Gandaki river on 11 October that damaged 200 houses, swept away five bridges and left five people missing.

Nine researchers from the UK, Nepal and India looked at areas up to 50km (30 miles) downstream from Himalayan rivers, as well as around 1,360 glacial lakes.

They found significant development in these areas - including an expansion of tourism facilities, infrastructure development and real estate.

It's clear in Pokhara, a major tourism hub at the foot of the Himalayas that's grown significantly in the past 30 years to cater for a massive increase in visitors.

Mayor Dhana Raj Acharya says it's a huge challenge to deal with the risk posed by the Seti Gandaki River, which stems from the Annapurna mountain range and flows right through the city. Many old buildings are just 5m (16ft) from river banks, he says, despite new rules requiring them to be further away.

"Where we move them, and how we do that, is the real challenge."

To the north is the world-renowned Annapurna trekking region that has also seen a major increase in settlements along river banks - some hit by recent floods and landslides .

Phurpa Chhiring Lama, who runs a homestay there, feels helpless. Normally all of his 20 rooms are occupied at this time of year - the peak trekking season - but now only five are. "We have been doing this business for more than 40 years, but we've never seen this kind of disaster."

Krishna Gauchan, whose hotel is close to the glacier-fed Modi river, is worried too. "This river can flood if the glacier collapses or if the glacial lake bursts out and we are living in constant fear."

Tourism investors promote some of these spots as destinations without factoring in the risks, suggests Khagendra Poudel, a geographer at a local campus of Tribhuvan University. It's similar to what's happening in parts of north India's Himalayan valleys which host major pilgrimages.

The president of the Hotel Association Pokhara admits tourism businesses have expanded "without any proper planning" in the region and been promoted "haphazardly".

"By the time disasters hit, it is too late," says Laxman Subedi. "As a professional body we are trying to create awareness among tourism entrepreneurs and investors."

But it's not just tourism. The regions surrounding the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers have seen a significant rise in the construction of hydropower plants .

"As river valleys become increasingly populated, development decisions being made today will shape disaster risk for decades to come," warns the study's lead author, University of Leeds glaciologist C Scott Watson.

And even more buildings may be under threat than those identified by the researchers.

The study categorised buildings at risk as all those that were within 50 vertical metres (164ft) of a river or glacial lake's surface.

But during the catastrophic flooding on 26 August, locals in Rasuwa district say the river level had risen by 70m (230ft) at some points - so even buildings that were relatively far from the river banks were hit and buried by debris-sludge.

The risks in all of these areas are largely driven by warming in the Himalayan region, which scientists say is happening at twice the global rate. This has sped up the melting of glaciers, icefields, snowpacks, and ground that's normally frozen all year.

This can, in turn, destabilize mountain slopes which are also frequently shaken by earthquakes, unleashing devastating disasters downstream.

The rapid melting is also filling up and expanding glacial lakes until they burst, causing deadly floods. Nepal alone has documented around 30 of these events since 1940.

Another issue is that rising temperatures cause rain to reach high altitudes where it used to only snow, leading to slope failures, rock and ice falls, and other disasters.

Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah raised the dangers of climate change at his recent UN General Assembly speech, where he said his country was paying a "colossal price" for a crisis it did not create.

"Every major disaster threatens to erase years of development. And it forces a poor country to borrow money to repair damage it did not cause."

Alton Byers, a mountain geographer at the University of Colorado who was not involved in the study, says it should serve as a "springboard" to bring about more effective early-warning systems and other precautionary measures.

But achieving that will be a challenge. Campaigners say building regulations aren't implemented on the ground and through the years, development has been haphazard in too many places.

Roads, hydropower projects, hotels and market towns have expanded on the low, flat land along rivers, which is accessible and buildable, says Prof Surya Raj Acharya, an urban planning expert and registrar at the University of Nepal.

Those responsible have often ignored safeguards including keeping off the river bank, he adds.

"A fragile ecosystem like the Himalaya demands stricter planning and building regulations than elsewhere, yet these rules have been weak and poorly enforced."

Authorities in Nepal say they are working to address these issues. Settlements within 15m (49ft) of the riverbank along the recently devastated Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi corridor will soon be banned, according to the national disaster agency. Similar rules are being introduced in other river corridors soon.

"It is a challenging job because people in many places have sentimental attachments with their land and property but we cannot ignore the increasing risks," says chief executive Dharam Raj Uprety.

A similar story has unfolded across Nepal's western border in India's Uttarakhand state, where maximum tourism limits and environmental regulations have been bypassed in the name of economic growth, claims activist Anoop Nautiyal.

On paper there are zoning rules prohibiting the construction of houses and infrastructure too close to river banks, "but on the ground we see no implementation of such rules.

The Uttarakhand government on 12 October approved new floodplain zoning rules to regulate land use and development. "Its objective is to protect life, property and important infrastructure from possible flood damage while maintaining the natural flow of flood waters," the state's cabinet decision read.

But Basanta Raj Adhikari, director of the Centre for Disaster Studies at Tribuvan University, thinks it will not be possible to mitigate such threats completely.

Insurance grades, he suggests, could be another way to encourage people to build in less risky areas. If authorities were to map places as high, moderate and low risk, he believes insurance coverage would "follow accordingly" ensuring people who build homes in safer areas get better protection.

But for now, the pace of construction across the region shows no signs of slowing.

India and China aren't friends - but Nepal wants to unite them against climate threats

Many Nepalis swept away in the floods aren't officially dead, leaving families in limbo
